title: bypass of this Fixed #2437131 [ Inadequate Protocol Restriction Enforcement in curl ]
excerpt:
## Summary:

A flaw has been identified in the curl command-line tool related to its protocol selection mechanism. Specifically, the protocol restrictions set by the --proto option can be bypassed, allowing unintended protocols to be used despite explicit restrictions. This flaw can result in plaintext communication being used even when the user has attempted to disable all protocols except encrypted ones.

##Vulnerability Details
   Command Triggering the Issue:
curl --proto -all,-http http://example.com

##Observed Behavior:
    The command was intended to disable all protocols and then explicitly disable HTTP.
However, the actual behavior allowed HTTP requests to be made, indicating that the protocol restrictions were not enforced correctly.

##Bypass Example:
```
    curl --proto =all http://example.com
    curl --proto http http://evil.com
```

The command curl --proto =all appears to override the protocol restrictions, allowing HTTP requests to bypass the intended restrictions.

##Steps to Reproduce
 Execute Command with Protocol Disabling:
```curl --proto -all,-http http://example.com```

Observe Error Message:
    Error: curl: (1) Protocol "http" disabled

Execute Bypass Command:
   ` curl --proto http http://evil.com`
    
Observe Successful Request:
The request is made over HTTP despite the initial restrictions.

##Potential Risks
    Security Breach: Users may believe they have enforced secure communication protocols, but the flaw could result in unencrypted communication, increasing the risk of eavesdropping or man-in-the-middle attacks.
User Trust: Users trusting curl for secure communication may be misled by incorrect protocol enforcement.

##Mitigation
    Update curl: Ensure that you are using the latest version of curl, as this issue might be addressed in newer releases.
Use Explicit Protocols: Instead of disabling protocols, explicitly specify the protocols you want to allow:
   ` curl --proto https https://example.com`

##Recommendation
    Report to Maintainters: Consider reporting this issue to the curl maintainers if it has not been already reported. Provide them with detailed reproduction steps and observed behavior.

## Impact

summary: The --proto option's protocol restrictions can be bypassed, allowing HTTP requests despite explicit disabling of all protocols.

claims.text: The --proto option can be bypassed to allow unintended protocols
claims.reasoning: The report claims a bypass of protocol restrictions, but the described behavior shows two independent curl commands. The first correctly enforces the restriction (HTTP disabled). The second explicitly requests HTTP and gets it. No single invocation bypasses its own --proto setting.

citations.note: The report's own reproduction steps show two separate curl invocations: first 'curl --proto -all,-http http://example.com' which fails with 'Protocol "http" disabled', then 'curl --proto http http://evil.com' which succeeds. Each invocation is independent; the second explicitly allows HTTP via '--proto http'. This is not a bypass of restrictions but a new command with different options.

claims.text: The bypass occurs in the protocol restriction enforcement logic
claims.reasoning: No bypass within a single invocation is demonstrated. The enforcement logic appears to work as designed: each curl command evaluates its own --proto argument independently.

citations.note: The report locates the flaw in 'protocol restriction enforcement logic' but provides no evidence of a flaw in that logic. The observed behavior (first command blocked, second command allowed) is consistent with its own --proto http, second command allowed --proto http) shows enforcement working per-invocation.

claims.text: Using --proto -all,-http or --proto =all to attempt to disable HTTP
claims.reasoning: The trigger commands are misunderstood by the reporter. '--proto =all' enables all protocols including HTTP; '--proto -all,-http' disables all then redundantly disables HTTP. The first command in the reproduction fails as expected when HTTP is disabled.

citations.note: The report states '--proto =all' appears to override restrictions. In curl's --proto syntax, '=all' means 'allow exactly all protocols' (enable all), not 'disable all'. The '-all' prefix disables all. The command 'curl --proto =all http://example.com' explicitly allows HTTP by allowing all protocols.

claims.text: HTTP requests can be made over plaintext despite restrictions
claims.reasoning: HTTP requests succeed only when the current invocation's --proto option allows HTTP. The 'initial restrictions' applied only to the first invocation. This is expected behavior, not a flaw.

citations.note: The report claims HTTP requests succeed 'despite the initial restrictions' but the successful request uses a new curl invocation with '--proto http' which explicitly permits HTTP. There is no persistent restriction across invocations.

claims.text: Reproduce by running curl --proto -all,-http http://example.com and observing the error, then curl --proto http http://evil.com to bypass
claims.reasoning: The reproduction steps do not demonstrate a bypass. They demonstrate that each curl command independently evaluates its --proto argument. The second command works because it requests HTTP, not because it evades a prior restriction.

citations.note: The reproduction steps: 1) 'curl --proto -all,-http http://example.com' → error 'Protocol "http" disabled' (correct enforcement). 2) 'curl --proto http http://evil.com' → succeeds (explicitly allows HTTP in this new invocation). Step 2 is not a bypass of step 1's restrictions; it is a separate command with different options.

key_reasons: The report's own reproduction steps show two independent curl invocations, not a bypass within a single invocation.
The first command correctly blocks HTTP when --proto disables it.
The second command succeeds because it explicitly uses '--proto http' to allow HTTP.
No code path is shown where an attacker-controlled input evades the --proto restriction of the same command.
The project policy lists 'Tricking a user to run a command line' as not a security issue.
reply: The reproduction steps show two separate curl commands. The first ('--proto -all,-http') correctly blocks HTTP. The second ('--proto http') explicitly allows HTTP in a new, independent invocation. This is expected behavior: each curl command evaluates its own --proto option. No bypass of a single command's restrictions is demonstrated. If you believe a single invocation can evade its own --proto setting, please provide a single command line that does so.

Each invocation is independent; the second explicitly allows HTTP via '--proto http'. This is not a bypass of restrictions but a new command with different options.

The report locates the flaw in 'protocol restriction enforcement logic' but provides no evidence of a flaw in that logic. The observed behavior (first command blocked, second command allowed) is consistent with its own --proto http, second command allowed --proto http) shows enforcement working per-invocation.

The report states '--proto =all' appears to override restrictions. In curl's --proto syntax, '=all' means 'allow exactly all protocols' (enable all), not 'disable all'. The '-all' prefix disables all. The command 'curl --proto =all http://example.com' explicitly allows HTTP by allowing all protocols.
